items.title: A Network Called "Resistance": An Interview with Autistici/Inventati
items.body:
Audio version from Molotov Now!



https://kolektiva.media/w/tndTXZDnPfAmm8Ka6yGimT 



Originally Published 8/31/26 - 3L23PM PST
Updated PIR Responses 8/31/26 - 6:35PM PST
Updated Banca Etica Statement 9/01/26 - 3:02AM PST

Editor’s note

This interview was conducted in writing with Autistici/Inventati following its August 26, 2026 designation by the United States under Executive Order 13224.

Sabot Media is an independent publication. We are not affiliated with A/I, do not represent the collective and did not conduct this interview at its direction. We are not fundraising for A/I, transmitting donations, providing technical or other services, mirroring its infrastructure, operating replacement services or archiving Noblogs material.

The interview has been edited only for spelling, punctuation, formatting and clarity. Any substantive condensation or reordering is identified. Links and brief explanatory context added by the editors appear in brackets. A/I was given the opportunity to review its own words for factual accuracy; it did not exercise editorial control over our introduction, reporting, questions or conclusions.

Statements by A/I represent the collective’s position. Claims concerning third parties are attributed accordingly and should not be read as independently verified unless our accompanying reporting says otherwise.

We sent separate questions to Public Interest Registry, Banca Etica, PayPal, The US Treasury Department and The US State Department. Their responses, where received, and their status as of publication appear below and will be updated as needed.

Interview with Autistici/Inventati

Immediate response and consequences

1. When and how did A/I first learn about the U.S. designation, and how did the collective initially respond?

A/I response:

We first learned about the designation via a tweet on Marco Rubio’s X account. We then did a bit of digging on the Treasury and State Department websites and eventually found the official announcements. The first thing we did was write a short statement to counter the allegations and start spreading it as widely as possible.

Then we had to check whether we had any assets in the United States, and we set about moving everything to different jurisdictions. We did not think PIR would act so swiftly, so we focused on domain registrars—we still had some things with a U.S.-based registrar—and PayPal. Apart from that, we thought we would be rather safe.

Then we had to answer hundreds of emails and interview requests, set up a coordinated response plan, and find lawyers as well as a press office. None of this proved quick to do, and we are still trying to juggle everything.

2. Since the designation, what consequences have already materialized—financially, technologically, institutionally or socially?

A/I response:

Our PayPal account has been closed for good, and we have been notified about it. To explain its decision, PayPal mentioned the designation of A/I by the U.S. authorities in the email it sent two days after terminating our account.

Autistici.org is also gone for good, and nobody felt the need to notify us. Our bank account is still active at the moment, but today is Sunday, August 30, and bank offices in Italy are closed. We sent an official legal warning to the bank not to close the account, and we have a call with the bank and our lawyers on Monday, August 31. We will see whether it has decided to reconsider its decision.

3. Have you seen banks, technology companies, hosting providers or other institutions over-comply by taking actions beyond what the sanctions clearly require?

Yes. Banca Etica’s reported decision to close our account illustrates how de-risking operates. The United States did not need to issue a direct order to the bank, and it has not been established that Italian law requires the relationship to be terminated. The bank can decide that maintaining the relationship creates too much legal, financial or reputational risk because our OFAC entry carries a secondary-sanctions warning.

We believe something similar occurred with our domain, although the exact chain of responsibility has not yet been publicly established. We attribute the intervention to PIR, but PIR has not publicly stated why it acted or whether OFAC instructed it to do so.

This is one of the central dangers of the designation. The United States does not need to order every company individually to abandon us. It can create enough uncertainty and fear that institutions impose the isolation themselves.

4. How has the designation affected ordinary A/I and Noblogs users, including people who have no relationship to any organization named by the U.S. government?

A/I response:

We covered this point in an update on our blog. In any case, mailboxes are working: our users just need to access them through a different server address. The @autistici.org mailboxes will be replaced with a different domain, but we are still implementing this step. In the meantime, the owners of these mailboxes can create an alias with a different domain and use that alias to send and receive email.

As for mailing lists created with the autistici.org domain, we moved all of them to a different domain and, as of today, they should be working. Noblogs.org has not been affected by the U.S. government’s decision, but it was compromised and we are trying to restore and secure it, as detailed on our blog.

5. What effects have been more difficult for outsiders to see? Are there quieter forms of isolation, fear or self-censorship that may never appear in an official record?

A/I response:

As for quieter effects, someone commented that you discover how much an infrastructure means to you and your life as soon as it disappears, and we think this will prove true.

We also think we are only seeing the short-term effects, since we cannot possibly know what the implications of this decision will be for U.S. citizens who use our services or connect with us for other reasons. While we were seeking legal advice, a U.S. lawyer recommended that U.S. citizens and U.S.-based organizations seek a legal opinion about the effects of the U.S. government’s decision. We cannot comment much further than this at the moment.

Infrastructure, political commitment and state power

6. The U.S. government describes A/I as part of the operational infrastructure of designated groups. What does that description misunderstand—or deliberately distort—about A/I and the services you provide?

It distorts the difference between providing communications infrastructure and directing what people do with it.

We are a volunteer-run Italian collective that has provided email, hosting, mailing lists, chat, videoconferencing, streaming and tools for privacy and anonymity since 2001. Our purpose is to make digital self-defense and free communication available to activists, individuals, groups and associations.

We have never claimed to be politically neutral. We are antifascist, antiracist, antisexist, antimilitarist, anticapitalist and opposed to authoritarianism. We select projects according to their compatibility with those principles. But political affinity does not mean that we direct, control or participate in everything users communicate through our infrastructure.

Our services are managed through a legally recognized association with legal responsibilities, contractual relationships and obligations under Italian law. Previous proceedings concerning third-party use of our infrastructure did not establish that we were responsible for users’ activity. We have fulfilled the legal obligations applicable to the services we provide.

The U.S. government is attempting to transform the existence of politically committed infrastructure into evidence of participation in every action associated with its users.

7. A/I has never claimed to be a politically neutral service provider. What does it mean to offer infrastructure based on political affinity without directing, controlling or participating in everything users do with it?

A/I response:

We never look into what users do with our infrastructure. Once an account has been created, we act as a mere conduit. As for mailing lists and mail accounts, we open accounts as soon as we have confirmed that requesters have accepted our Terms of Service and manifesto and respect our policy.

On Noblogs, we do not even ask for that, since anyone who has a mail account on our servers—or on other privacy-friendly servers we trust—is free to open a blog. In any case, we do not know our account owners’ identities and ask them not to disclose their identities to us under any circumstances.

We believe users and readers will notify us if someone violates our policy while using our services. We would certainly act if we received an official legal order to shut down an account that violates a law; in such cases, we are bound to comply with existing regulations.

8. Is the government collapsing the distinction between a communications provider and the people who communicate through it? What precedent would that establish for other independent providers?

Yes. That collapse is at the center of the designation.

The accusation is not simply that we carried out a particular attack. The United States argues that providing email, hosting, chat, streaming, encryption and other technological services can constitute material support when those services are used by people or organizations it has designated.

That reasoning shifts responsibility from the person carrying out an action to the provider maintaining the infrastructure through which people communicate.

The precedent extends far beyond A/I. The same theory could be used against email providers, hosting projects, cloud services, encrypted messaging systems, payment processors and domain registrars. It encourages providers to monitor, investigate and exclude users—and to terminate entire services whenever they fear that one user may create sanctions exposure.

9. Earlier attacks targeted particular servers, disks and accounts. This designation instead targets the financial, technological and institutional relationships surrounding A/I. How does that change the nature of the threat?

Earlier attacks often focused on a particular machine, account or piece of data. We responded by distributing our infrastructure, encrypting information and designing services capable of continuing when a server was seized or a provider became hostile.

This attack operates at several external layers simultaneously. A domain can be removed from normal DNS resolution. A bank can close an account. A payment processor can block transactions. Registrars, hosts and technology providers can withdraw because they fear sanctions exposure.

We can control and protect our machines, but we do not control the .org registry, international banking networks, payment systems or every company connecting our infrastructure to the wider internet.

The objective is no longer simply to seize a server. It is to make the collective institutionally and economically untouchable.

10. What does it mean when encryption, minimal logging and privacy protections are treated as evidence of criminal intent rather than forms of digital self-defense?

A/I response:

They cannot accept that someone would open their own house to random people so they can freely build their own tools and narratives and speak for themselves. As much as they boast of their respect for free speech and individual rights, the United States cannot think beyond the power of money and the need to control what other people want to do and how they want to live their lives.

We think people are responsible for what they do, and they deserve the opportunity to struggle for a better life, for a better world and to overcome injustice. We think that providing infrastructure that lets them explain how they plan to do that, and find others who share the same ideas, is worth our time, effort and all the work we put into it. Names and identities have nothing to do with this.

11. Why do you think autonomous communications infrastructure has become such an important target now?

A/I response:

We think the U.S. government wanted to make a point. The United States—and Trump specifically—destroyed multilateralism and international diplomacy, together with any sense that shared rules are for everyone to abide by. They are saying they own the infosphere and all networks.

Unfortunately, we do not think this will spark a movement toward recognizing networks and communications as a common good above individual states and jurisdictions. Instead, it will ignite a move by every powerful country to grab a piece of the cake and steal it from the others—which is the exact opposite of the original idea behind global networking.

It is the same thing we have seen in the financial sphere: globalize poverty and exploitation, privatize gain and privilege. Then again, We think they also wanted to target political activities that damage their image and their projects for the future of the United States. Hitting us was just a means, not an end in itself. At least, that is part of what we are dealing with now: the fallout.

12. What does this action reveal about the power of the United States to isolate a small, non-U.S. collective through banks and private technology companies?

The designation does not automatically make us illegal in Italy or throughout the European Union. The United States, Italy and the European Union maintain distinct legal systems and sanctions lists.

But formal jurisdiction is only part of the story. Our OFAC entry carries a secondary-sanctions warning. Banks and technology companies outside the United States may fear losing access to American markets, dollar transactions, correspondent banking or U.S.-based services if they continue dealing with us.

That fear turns private companies into enforcers of American foreign policy. The United States does not need to issue a direct order to every Italian bank, registrar or technology provider. It can create a compliance risk, and institutions will isolate us to protect themselves.

The mechanism is:

OFAC designation → compliance risk → institutional de-risking → termination of services

This is how a decision made in Washington can produce immediate consequences for a small collective operating legally in Italy.

13. The designation repeatedly connects antifascism with terrorism. How do you understand that political move, and whom is it intended to frighten beyond A/I?

A/I response:

As I said above, this move clearly targets everyone who radically opposes the U.S. government, everyone who thinks what it is doing is wrong and should be challenged and stopped.

I do not think it is only about antifa groups—not to mention that declaring yourself against antifascists makes you an anti-antifascist, which means a fascist by definition, does it not? We think this decision also targets less militant people who want to be part of a general opposition to the current new U.S. authoritarianism, its vision and its project.

14. If this designation is allowed to stand without serious resistance, who or what do you believe may be targeted next?

A/I response:

The next infrastructure social movements use? But we think large commercial infrastructure providers should realize that this precedent is a very real danger for them too. What if anti-ICE movements used Google Sites? Would the United States then ask Google to shut down their accounts? Would it ban Google altogether?

A/I’s history and political vision

15. At A/I’s founding, the least technically experienced participant was deliberately placed at the keyboard. What does that story say about the relationship between knowledge and power?

A/I response:

We firmly believe everyone should be empowered to take technology into their own hands. We started this project because we also wanted to learn, and we have come a loooong way over these twenty-five years. Of course, not all of us are as technically knowledgeable as others, but we learn, we struggle and we try to include each one of us so that we can all take up necessary tasks.

Politics has to do with objectives; technology has to do with means. But there is no technology without political implications. We once used to say, “Technical problems do not exist; they are excuses.” Maybe this is a bit too much, but it means that one should always consider the goals first and only afterward decide how to achieve them. We should always think about what political goals we want to achieve through technology.

16. A/I’s history repeatedly follows a pattern: disclose the attack, repair the damage, share the lesson and build something harder to destroy. Can the present attack be transformed in the same way?

A/I response:

I would really like to say, “Of course,” and we will try as hard as we can. But this is very big, and it is an attack on the fundamentally free structure of the internet that exposes its partiality and widespread privatization.

Some of the things happening now were theoretical threats we knew about, but the measures needed to prevent them were far beyond our capabilities. We cannot become a supranational domain manager 

We will try to do our best. Everyone should try, just as we will. The first person who finds the solution should share it, and we should run ahead of these people who can think only in terms of power and destruction.

Preservation and solidarity

17. What responses since the designation have felt genuinely useful or meaningful to the collective?

A/I response:

Solidarity has been huge, and we are very grateful. Actions, contributions and articles created in good faith to support us cannot be harmful. Some people have tried to use this situation to promote themselves or taunt others, but I suppose that tells you more about them than about us.

18. What should people in the United States understand before attempting donations, technical assistance, mirroring or other forms of direct support?

A/I response:

We still do not have a clear answer to that. We have been talking with lawyers from EFF to obtain a clear statement. At the moment, we understand that until September 25 nothing changes. After that date, U.S.-based citizens should seek legal counsel to evaluate the risks of getting in touch with us in any way. We are not sure whether this applies simply to using our services.

Editor’s note: This reflects A/I’s understanding at the time of the interview and is not legal advice.

We ask everybody to be very careful because we do not want anyone to be harmed. Your lives and freedom mean more than our network. This has always been true and always will be. Stay human, before and above anything else.

19. What can journalists, researchers, publishers and digital-rights organizations do independently and responsibly?

A/I response:

They have to speak up, take a stand, and push every decision-maker and policymaker to intervene and pressure the U.S. government to reverse its decision. Audio version from Molotov Now!



https://kolektiva.media/w/tndTXZDnPfAmm8Ka6yGimT 



Originally Published 8/31/26 - 3L23PM PST
Updated PIR Responses 8/31/26 - 6:35PM PST
Updated Banca Etica Statement 9/01/26 - 3:02AM PST

Editor’s note

This interview was conducted in writing with Autistici/Inventati following its August 26, 2026 designation by the United States under Executive Order 13224.

Sabot Media is an independent publication. We are not affiliated with A/I, do not represent the collective and did not conduct this interview at its direction. We are not fundraising for A/I, transmitting donations, providing technical or other services, mirroring its infrastructure, operating replacement services or archiving Noblogs material.

The interview has been edited only for spelling, punctuation, formatting and clarity. Any substantive condensation or reordering is identified. Links and brief explanatory context added by the editors appear in brackets. A/I was given the opportunity to review its own words for factual accuracy; it did not exercise editorial control over our introduction, reporting, questions or conclusions.

Statements by A/I represent the collective’s position. Claims concerning third parties are attributed accordingly and should not be read as independently verified unless our accompanying reporting says otherwise.

We sent separate questions to Public Interest Registry, Banca Etica, PayPal, The US Treasury Department and The US State Department. Their responses, where received, and their status as of publication appear below and will be updated as needed.

Interview with Autistici/Inventati

Immediate response and consequences

1. When and how did A/I first learn about the U.S. designation, and how did the collective initially respond?

A/I response:

We first learned about the designation via a tweet on Marco Rubio’s X account. We then did a bit of digging on the Treasury and State Department websites and eventually found the official announcements. The first thing we did was write a short statement to counter the allegations and start spreading it as widely as possible.

Then we had to check whether we had any assets in the United States, and we set about moving everything to different jurisdictions. We did not think PIR would act so swiftly, so we focused on domain registrars—we still had some things with a U.S.-based registrar—and PayPal. Apart from that, we thought we would be rather safe.

Then we had to answer hundreds of emails and interview requests, set up a coordinated response plan, and find lawyers as well as a press office. None of this proved quick to do, and we are still trying to juggle everything.

2. Since the designation, what consequences have already materialized—financially, technologically, institutionally or socially?

A/I response:

Our PayPal account has been closed for good, and we have been notified about it. To explain its decision, PayPal mentioned the designation of A/I by the U.S. authorities in the email it sent two days after terminating our account.

Autistici.org is also gone for good, and nobody felt the need to notify us. Our bank account is still active at the moment, but today is Sunday, August 30, and bank offices in Italy are closed. We sent an official legal warning to the bank not to close the account, and we have a call with the bank and our lawyers on Monday, August 31. We will see whether it has decided to reconsider its decision.

3. Have you seen banks, technology companies, hosting providers or other institutions over-comply by taking actions beyond what the sanctions clearly require?

Yes. Banca Etica’s reported decision to close our account illustrates how de-risking operates. The United States did not need to issue a direct order to the bank, and it has not been established that Italian law requires the relationship to be terminated. The bank can decide that maintaining the relationship creates too much legal, financial or reputational risk because our OFAC entry carries a secondary-sanctions warning.

We believe something similar occurred with our domain, although the exact chain of responsibility has not yet been publicly established. We attribute the intervention to PIR, but PIR has not publicly stated why it acted or whether OFAC instructed it to do so.

This is one of the central dangers of the designation. The United States does not need to order every company individually to abandon us. It can create enough uncertainty and fear that institutions impose the isolation themselves.

4. How has the designation affected ordinary A/I and Noblogs users, including people who have no relationship to any organization named by the U.S. government?

A/I response:

We covered this point in an update on our blog. In any case, mailboxes are working: our users just need to access them through a different server address. The @autistici.org mailboxes will be replaced with a different domain, but we are still implementing this step. In the meantime, the owners of these mailboxes can create an alias with a different domain and use that alias to send and receive email.

As for mailing lists created with the autistici.org domain, we moved all of them to a different domain and, as of today, they should be working. Noblogs.org has not been affected by the U.S. government’s decision, but it was compromised and we are trying to restore and secure it, as detailed on our blog.

5. What effects have been more difficult for outsiders to see? Are there quieter forms of isolation, fear or self-censorship that may never appear in an official record?

A/I response:

As for quieter effects, someone commented that you discover how much an infrastructure means to you and your life as soon as it disappears, and we think this will prove true.

We also think we are only seeing the short-term effects, since we cannot possibly know what the implications of this decision will be for U.S. citizens who use our services or connect with us for other reasons. While we were seeking legal advice, a U.S. lawyer recommended that U.S. citizens and U.S.-based organizations seek a legal opinion about the effects of the U.S. government’s decision. We cannot comment much further than this at the moment.

Infrastructure, political commitment and state power

6. The U.S. government describes A/I as part of the operational infrastructure of designated groups. What does that description misunderstand—or deliberately distort—about A/I and the services you provide?

It distorts the difference between providing communications infrastructure and directing what people do with it.

We are a volunteer-run Italian collective that has provided email, hosting, mailing lists, chat, videoconferencing, streaming and tools for privacy and anonymity since 2001. Our purpose is to make digital self-defense and free communication available to activists, individuals, groups and associations.

We have never claimed to be politically neutral. We are antifascist, antiracist, antisexist, antimilitarist, anticapitalist and opposed to authoritarianism. We select projects according to their compatibility with those principles. But political affinity does not mean that we direct, control or participate in everything users communicate through our infrastructure.

Our services are managed through a legally recognized association with legal responsibilities, contractual relationships and obligations under Italian law. Previous proceedings concerning third-party use of our infrastructure did not establish that we were responsible for users’ activity. We have fulfilled the legal obligations applicable to the services we provide.

The U.S. government is attempting to transform the existence of politically committed infrastructure into evidence of participation in every action associated with its users.

7. A/I has never claimed to be a politically neutral service provider. What does it mean to offer infrastructure based on political affinity without directing, controlling or participating in everything users do with it?

A/I response:

We never look into what users do with our infrastructure. Once an account has been created, we act as a mere conduit. As for mailing lists and mail accounts, we open accounts as soon as we have confirmed that requesters have accepted our Terms of Service and manifesto and respect our policy.

On Noblogs, we do not even ask for that, since anyone who has a mail account on our servers—or on other privacy-friendly servers we trust—is free to open a blog. In any case, we do not know our account owners’ identities and ask them not to disclose their identities to us under any circumstances.

We believe users and readers will notify us if someone violates our policy while using our services. We would certainly act if we received an official legal order to shut down an account that violates a law; in such cases, we are bound to comply with existing regulations.

8. Is the government collapsing the distinction between a communications provider and the people who communicate through it? What precedent would that establish for other independent providers?

Yes. That collapse is at the center of the designation.

The accusation is not simply that we carried out a particular attack. The United States argues that providing email, hosting, chat, streaming, encryption and other technological services can constitute material support when those services are used by people or organizations it has designated.

That reasoning shifts responsibility from the person carrying out an action to the provider maintaining the infrastructure through which people communicate.

The precedent extends far beyond A/I. The same theory could be used against email providers, hosting projects, cloud services, encrypted messaging systems, payment processors and domain registrars. It encourages providers to monitor, investigate and exclude users—and to terminate entire services whenever they fear that one user may create sanctions exposure.

9. Earlier attacks targeted particular servers, disks and accounts. This designation instead targets the financial, technological and institutional relationships surrounding A/I. How does that change the nature of the threat?

Earlier attacks often focused on a particular machine, account or piece of data. We responded by distributing our infrastructure, encrypting information and designing services capable of continuing when a server was seized or a provider became hostile.

This attack operates at several external layers simultaneously. A domain can be removed from normal DNS resolution. A bank can close an account. A payment processor can block transactions. Registrars, hosts and technology providers can withdraw because they fear sanctions exposure.

We can control and protect our machines, but we do not control the .org registry, international banking networks, payment systems or every company connecting our infrastructure to the wider internet.

The objective is no longer simply to seize a server. It is to make the collective institutionally and economically untouchable.

10. What does it mean when encryption, minimal logging and privacy protections are treated as evidence of criminal intent rather than forms of digital self-defense?

A/I response:

They cannot accept that someone would open their own house to random people so they can freely build their own tools and narratives and speak for themselves. As much as they boast of their respect for free speech and individual rights, the United States cannot think beyond the power of money and the need to control what other people want to do and how they want to live their lives.

We think people are responsible for what they do, and they deserve the opportunity to struggle for a better life, for a better world and to overcome injustice. We think that providing infrastructure that lets them explain how they plan to do that, and find others who share the same ideas, is worth our time, effort and all the work we put into it. Names and identities have nothing to do with this.

11. Why do you think autonomous communications infrastructure has become such an important target now?

A/I response:

We think the U.S. government wanted to make a point. The United States—and Trump specifically—destroyed multilateralism and international diplomacy, together with any sense that shared rules are for everyone to abide by. They are saying they own the infosphere and all networks.

Unfortunately, we do not think this will spark a movement toward recognizing networks and communications as a common good above individual states and jurisdictions. Instead, it will ignite a move by every powerful country to grab a piece of the cake and steal it from the others—which is the exact opposite of the original idea behind global networking.

It is the same thing we have seen in the financial sphere: globalize poverty and exploitation, privatize gain and privilege. Then again, We think they also wanted to target political activities that damage their image and their projects for the future of the United States. Hitting us was just a means, not an end in itself. At least, that is part of what we are dealing with now: the fallout.

12. What does this action reveal about the power of the United States to isolate a small, non-U.S. collective through banks and private technology companies?

The designation does not automatically make us illegal in Italy or throughout the European Union. The United States, Italy and the European Union maintain distinct legal systems and sanctions lists.

But formal jurisdiction is only part of the story. Our OFAC entry carries a secondary-sanctions warning. Banks and technology companies outside the United States may fear losing access to American markets, dollar transactions, correspondent banking or U.S.-based services if they continue dealing with us.

That fear turns private companies into enforcers of American foreign policy. The United States does not need to issue a direct order to every Italian bank, registrar or technology provider. It can create a compliance risk, and institutions will isolate us to protect themselves.

The mechanism is:

OFAC designation → compliance risk → institutional de-risking → termination of services

This is how a decision made in Washington can produce immediate consequences for a small collective operating legally in Italy.

13. The designation repeatedly connects antifascism with terrorism. How do you understand that political move, and whom is it intended to frighten beyond A/I?

A/I response:

As I said above, this move clearly targets everyone who radically opposes the U.S. government, everyone who thinks what it is doing is wrong and should be challenged and stopped.

I do not think it is only about antifa groups—not to mention that declaring yourself against antifascists makes you an anti-antifascist, which means a fascist by definition, does it not? We think this decision also targets less militant people who want to be part of a general opposition to the current new U.S. authoritarianism, its vision and its project.

14. If this designation is allowed to stand without serious resistance, who or what do you believe may be targeted next?

A/I response:

The next infrastructure social movements use? But we think large commercial infrastructure providers should realize that this precedent is a very real danger for them too. What if anti-ICE movements used Google Sites? Would the United States then ask Google to shut down their accounts? Would it ban Google altogether?

A/I’s history and political vision

15. At A/I’s founding, the least technically experienced participant was deliberately placed at the keyboard. What does that story say about the relationship between knowledge and power?

A/I response:

We firmly believe everyone should be empowered to take technology into their own hands. We started this project because we also wanted to learn, and we have come a loooong way over these twenty-five years. Of course, not all of us are as technically knowledgeable as others, but we learn, we struggle and we try to include each one of us so that we can all take up necessary tasks.

Politics has to do with objectives; technology has to do with means. But there is no technology without political implications. We once used to say, “Technical problems do not exist; they are excuses.” Maybe this is a bit too much, but it means that one should always consider the goals first and only afterward decide how to achieve them. We should always think about what political goals we want to achieve through technology.

16. A/I’s history repeatedly follows a pattern: disclose the attack, repair the damage, share the lesson and build something harder to destroy. Can the present attack be transformed in the same way?

A/I response:

I would really like to say, “Of course,” and we will try as hard as we can. But this is very big, and it is an attack on the fundamentally free structure of the internet that exposes its partiality and widespread privatization.

Some of the things happening now were theoretical threats we knew about, but the measures needed to prevent them were far beyond our capabilities. We cannot become a supranational domain manager 

We will try to do our best. Everyone should try, just as we will. The first person who finds the solution should share it, and we should run ahead of these people who can think only in terms of power and destruction.

Preservation and solidarity

17. What responses since the designation have felt genuinely useful or meaningful to the collective?

A/I response:

Solidarity has been huge, and we are very grateful. Actions, contributions and articles created in good faith to support us cannot be harmful. Some people have tried to use this situation to promote themselves or taunt others, but I suppose that tells you more about them than about us.

18. What should people in the United States understand before attempting donations, technical assistance, mirroring or other forms of direct support?

A/I response:

We still do not have a clear answer to that. We have been talking with lawyers from EFF to obtain a clear statement. At the moment, we understand that until September 25 nothing changes. After that date, U.S.-based citizens should seek legal counsel to evaluate the risks of getting in touch with us in any way. We are not sure whether this applies simply to using our services.

Editor’s note: This reflects A/I’s understanding at the time of the interview and is not legal advice.

We ask everybody to be very careful because we do not want anyone to be harmed. Your lives and freedom mean more than our network. This has always been true and always will be. Stay human, before and above anything else.

19. What can journalists, researchers, publishers and digital-rights organizations do independently and responsibly?

A/I response:

They have to speak up, take a stand, and push every decision-maker and policymaker to intervene and pressure the U.S. government to reverse its decision. We need a global wave to mount, and we cannot create it alone. We are not that strong alone, but together we will prevail. How did that song go? “We have been nought; we shall be all.”

A/I response:

This is a complex question, and I do not think we are able to answer it fully. To me, it would mean seeing thousands of structures similar to Autistici/Inventati be born and grow. Let us have a thousand servers, a thousand networks. Let us flood them with possibilities until they run out of time and money to pursue and persecute us.

A/I response:

How does this affect the status of the internet as a common good? Why can the United States decide such crucial things for the whole world? When is imperialism finally going to disappear? But maybe I am being a bit too dreamy here.

22. What would constitute survival—not merely keeping A/I’s servers online, but preserving the political project surrounding them?

A/I response:

We have to be able to keep doing what we do for everyone around the world. That is the objective. Will we be able to do it? I do not know, but we will give it our best shot. As always.

A/I response:

Resistance.

items.title: Jennie Bastian, founder of Communication
items.excerpt: No, Jennie Bastian did not invent communication as a concept. But she DID start a really cool punk venue by that name! Interested in riot grrl, political art, and social justice since her teen years, Jennie makes art about disability liberation, creates all-ages art spaces, and is a youth-liberationist parent of a five-year-old. In this episode, mk and Jennie chat about age inclusion in the punk scene, the role of art in social movements, and so much more. Hosted on Acast. See acast.com/privacy for more information.

items.title: Vicky Osterweil, Author of THE EXTENDED UNIVERSE
items.excerpt: Vicky Osterweil's book, as she puts it, seeks to answer two questions: "why are all superhero movies the same?" and "why did Disney lobby the Biden administration to stop them sharing the COVID vaccine with the third world in 2021?" THE EXTENDED UNIVERSE, her upcoming book, is all about the role of Disney in the nuclear family, ageism, and the state. On this podcast, we talk about media, trans health, and (yas) our childhoods projecting transness onto various Disney characters. Hosted on Acast. See acast.com/privacy for more information.

items.title: Lola Bloom, Transfeminine YouTube Influencer
items.excerpt: Lola Bloom on being trans online: "I think the space I aim to create would pave the way for trans kids to do similar work in an environment that isn't so hostile or alienating. I also think that giving people a space to exist and to be authentically themselves while they share skills and grow is integral to helping our community heal. It's incredibly difficult to transition and providing people the encouragement and resources they need is always my biggest success." Lola's Discord: https://discord.gg/aDMWFZMtz2 Hosted on Acast. items.title: Ashley Halliwell on Music & Neuroqueer Community
items.excerpt: "I could not even pretend to be neurotypical if I tried. So the neurodivergent community is very important to me. My fellow neurodivergents are my kin and my comrades, and we live anarchy day in and day out, even if we don't realize it. I think most of us would have a harder time trying to shove ourselves into capitalistic, neurotypical boxes than to let ourselves be free, if we all thought about it and did the work necessary to liberate ourselves and each other." items.excerpt: A NETWORK CALLED RESISTANCE: AN INTERVIEW WITH AUTISTICI/INVENTATI Days after the United States designated the twenty-five-year-old Italian communications collective Autistici/Inventati under Executive Order 13224, A/I answered Sabot Media’s questions about what happened next. Its PayPal account was terminated. Public Interest Registry suspended the autistici.org domain. Banca Etica temporarily suspended operations on its bank account. Ordinary users were forced to reroute email accounts and mailing lists as the effects of a decision made in Washington spread through private financial and tech
items.body:
Read the full interview


A NETWORK CALLED RESISTANCE: AN INTERVIEW WITH AUTISTICI/INVENTATI


Days after the United States designated the twenty-five-year-old Italian communications collective Autistici/Inventati under Executive Order 13224, A/I answered Sabot Media’s questions about what happened next.


Its PayPal account was terminated. Public Interest Registry suspended the autistici.org domain. Banca Etica temporarily suspended operations on its bank account. Ordinary users were forced to reroute email accounts and mailing lists as the effects of a decision made in Washington spread through private financial and technological infrastructure.


In this audio edition of Sabot Media’s written interview, Molotov Now! host Sprout reads the questions and A/I’s written responses are rendered using a text-to-speech voice. The synthetic voice is an accessibility and production tool; it is not the voice of an A/I member or representative.


The collective discusses encryption, antifascism, autonomous infrastructure, the political meaning of privacy, institutional isolation and what it would mean to build “a thousand servers, a thousand networks.”


The episode concludes with a reflection from Sabot Media on the state’s attempt to make communications infrastructure punishable by association, the silence surrounding the designation and why a government blacklist will never decide whose stories we publish.


Read the complete interview and accompanying institutional responses:

https://sabot.media/post/a-network-called-resistance


Music: “What Is Freedom” by Sima Lee.


Sabot Media independently conducted and published this interview. We are not affiliated with Autistici/Inventati, do not represent the collective and are not acting at its direction.

items.title: Keep the Meals Coming: Food Not Bombs Gaza Builds a Lifeline in Deir al-Balah
items.body:
A few months ago, a message from someone we did not know arrived in Sabot Media’s Instagram inbox.

His name was Jamal Abu Al-Ata. He was writing from Gaza and asking for financial support for the mutual-aid work he was doing there. The message appeared to be part of a broad effort to reach anyone who might listen. We could not promise to send the money he was requesting, but we told him that, as a publisher, we might be able to help differently: interview him, share his reporting and appeals, and help more people find the work.

At first, Jamal was understandably unsure what Sabot Media was or what we were proposing. Over the following weeks, we continued talking through Instagram. We explained our work, learned more about his, and gradually built enough trust to move the conversation to WhatsApp. From there, we began discussing an interview and a larger solidarity campaign for Food Not Bombs Gaza.

Completing a conventional scheduled interview has not been easy. Time, connectivity, displacement, and the demands of organizing under war do not conform to a newsroom calendar. That does not mean Jamal lacks something to say. It means the form of the interview has to adapt to the conditions in which he is living.

This campaign is our attempt to do that.

Sabot has built Jamal a private, low-bandwidth correspondence room where he can answer questions with text, audio, photographs, or video whenever time and connection permit. He can keep a response private between us, publish it directly to the campaign, or return later to continue the conversation. Members of the public can submit questions, but Sabot reviews them before deciding what to forward.

The result will not be one interview conducted at one appointed hour. It will be an ongoing, asynchronous conversation in Jamal’s own words—alongside a durable archive of Food Not Bombs Gaza’s updates and a direct route to its fundraiser.

The story began with a message sent in the hope that somebody might answer. We answered. What follows is the work that grew from it.

Keep the Meals Coming: Food Not Bombs Gaza Builds a Lifeline in Deir al-Balah

Food Not Bombs Gaza is working under bombardment, displacement, extreme food prices, and worsening hunger to move bread and basic food directly to families in Deir al-Balah.

The Palestinian-led mutual-aid project is directed by Jamal Abu Al-Ata. Its recent field updates document both the material work of obtaining food and the conditions surrounding it: nearby bombing, dangerous movement, unstable markets, injured organizers, and families attempting to survive without dependable access to basic necessities.

On August 24, Food Not Bombs Gaza reported distributing 150 fresh bundles of bread to displaced families. The project said that brought the total provided through its recent consecutive distributions to 1,075 bundles.

Jamal reported carrying out the distribution despite an injury to his hand.

“If the world is silent in the face of this destruction, we will not be silent in the face of hunger,” he wrote.

The numbers are reported by Food Not Bombs Gaza through its public field updates. Sabot Media has not independently audited the purchases or distribution totals. The photographs, videos, captions, and continuing public record nevertheless show a project repeatedly organizing food distributions under extraordinary conditions.

Food in an unstable market

An August 13 appeal announced a $6,650 initiative to purchase and distribute food baskets to displaced families and children in camps around Deir al-Balah.

Food Not Bombs Gaza said the proposed baskets would contain staples including rice, sugar, cooking oil, salt, milk for children, beans, cheese, dates, lentils, potatoes, and other available necessities. Jamal estimated that each basket would cost approximately $65 to $70 and support a family for about one week.

The project warned that those estimates could change suddenly because prices and availability in Gaza remain unstable.

That distinction matters. The immediate need is not for supporters abroad to attempt to ship individual bags of flour or bottles of oil into Gaza. Food Not Bombs Gaza needs money that can be used locally, whenever food can be found, at prices that may change without warning.

Earlier reporting from the project shows the cumulative importance of smaller distributions. On June 25, Food Not Bombs Gaza said it had coordinated with a bakery in Deir al-Balah to obtain 215 bundles of fresh bread. Together with two preceding initiatives, it reported distributing 565 bundles over several days.

These are not abstract aid targets. They are attempts to shorten the distance between available food and families who cannot afford or safely reach it.

Mutual aid under bombardment

The work does not happen outside the war surrounding it.

On August 25, Jamal posted video from Deir al-Balah as smoke rose behind him. He reported ongoing bombing east of the city and explosions that did not stop.

“We live in constant danger and there is no safe place,” he wrote, “but despite all this bombing and fear, we cling to hope and life.”

Three days earlier, Jamal described nearby attacks, hunger, increasingly dangerous movement, and the psychological effects of repeated close calls on children and families. He nevertheless said Food Not Bombs Gaza was planning its next distribution.

The project’s updates do not present mutual aid as a substitute for political action or an answer to the destruction of Gaza. They show people refusing to abandon one another inside conditions they did not create and cannot solve alone.

Direct aid and an independent channel

Sabot Media is launching this campaign with Jamal’s knowledge and enthusiastic approval.

The campaign has two immediate purposes.

The first is to direct money toward the existing fundraiser supporting Food Not Bombs Gaza. Sabot does not collect the donations and takes no percentage. The current Chuffed campaign is organized by Kati Llewellyn for Jamal and his community. The organizer says funds are transferred to Jamal through USDT because conventional services such as PayPal impose significant fees and access barriers.

The second purpose is to give Jamal an independent place to continue publishing.

Instagram remains an important channel for Food Not Bombs Gaza, but commercial platforms can restrict, suspend, or erase accounts with little warning. Jamal now has access to a private Sabot contributor room where he can send text, photographs, audio, or video directly to Sabot—or deliberately publish an update to the campaign website himself.

Private correspondence remains private. Public dispatches are explicitly marked and appear on the campaign page under Jamal’s chosen identity. He can also withdraw or permanently delete his own publications.

The aim is not for Sabot to take possession of his story. It is to provide infrastructure Jamal can use: a stable campaign address, an independent dispatch archive, an ongoing asynchronous interview room, and a donation pathway that remains findable if an Instagram account or fundraising platform becomes unavailable.

What supporters can do

The simplest action is to donate through the verified fundraiser linked from the campaign page.

Supporters can also organize benefit shows, community meals, raffles, art sales, film screenings, and other local fundraisers. Food Not Bombs Gaza has specifically encouraged artists and supporters to create decentralized benefits. Sabot’s campaign includes a benefit studio for producing customized posters and social graphics tied to the stable campaign address.

Sharing Jamal’s updates matters. Moving money matters more.

Food Not Bombs Gaza is already doing the work: finding food, coordinating purchases, documenting distributions, and continuing under bombardment. The task outside Gaza is to provide the resources that allow that work to continue—and to help ensure Jamal’s voice cannot be removed by a platform’s decision.

Donate, read Jamal’s dispatches, or organize a benefit:
https://sabot.media/campaigns/food-not-bombs-gaza

Sources for the reported field claims:

  • August 25: bombing east of Deir al-Balah
  • August 24: 150 bread bundles and reported cumulative total
  • August 22: conditions and planned distribution
  • August 13: food-basket initiative
  • June 25: bakery coordination and earlier distributions
  • Current Chuffed fundraiser

Three days earlier, Jamal described nearby attacks, hunger, increasingly dangerous movement, and the psychological effects of repeated close calls on children and families. He nevertheless said Food Not Bombs Gaza was planning its next distribution.

The project’s updates do not present mutual aid as a substitute for political action or an answer to the destruction of Gaza. They show people refusing to abandon one another inside conditions they did not create and cannot solve alone.

Direct aid and an independent channel

Sabot Media is launching this campaign with Jamal’s knowledge and enthusiastic approval.

The campaign has two immediate purposes.

The first is to direct money toward the existing fundraiser supporting Food Not Bombs Gaza. Sabot does not collect the donations and takes no percentage. The current Chuffed campaign is organized by Kati Llewellyn for Jamal and his community. The organizer says funds are transferred to Jamal through USDT because conventional services such as PayPal impose significant fees and access barriers.

The second purpose is to give Jamal an independent place to continue publishing.

Instagram remains an important channel for Food Not Bombs Gaza, but commercial platforms can restrict, suspend, or erase accounts with little warning. Jamal now has access to a private Sabot contributor room where he can send text, photographs, audio, or video directly to Sabot—or deliberately publish an update to the campaign website himself.

Private correspondence remains private. Public dispatches are explicitly marked and appear on the campaign page under Jamal’s chosen identity. He can also withdraw or permanently delete his own publications.

The aim is not for Sabot to take possession of his story. It is to provide infrastructure Jamal can use: a stable campaign address, an independent dispatch archive, an ongoing asynchronous interview room, and a donation pathway that remains findable if an Instagram account or fundraising platform becomes unavailable.

What supporters can do

The simplest action is to donate through the verified fundraiser linked from the campaign page.

Supporters can also organize benefit shows, community meals, raffles, art sales, film screenings, and other local fundraisers. Food Not Bombs Gaza has specifically encouraged artists and supporters to create decentralized benefits. Sabot’s campaign includes a benefit studio for producing customized posters and social graphics tied to the stable campaign address.

Sharing Jamal’s updates matters. Moving money matters more.

Food Not Bombs Gaza is already doing the work: finding food, coordinating purchases, documenting distributions, and continuing under bombardment. The task outside Gaza is to provide the resources that allow that work to continue—and to help ensure Jamal’s voice cannot be removed by a platform’s decision.

Donate, read Jamal’s dispatches, or organize a benefit:
https://sabot.media/campaigns/food-not-bombs-gaza

Sources for the reported field claims:

  • August 25: bombing east of Deir al-Balah
  • August 24: 150 bread bundles and reported cumulative total
  • August 22: conditions and planned distribution
  • August 13: food-basket initiative
  • June 25: bakery coordination and earlier distributions
  • Current Chuffed fundraiser

items.title: Banca Etica Suspends A/I’s Account While Condemning the Sanctions Behind It
items.body:
The Italian bank says A/I’s account showed no previous anti-money-laundering concerns—but fears U.S. secondary sanctions could endanger services for 130,000 customers and members.

What follows is a English language translation of Banca Etica's (Ethical Bank's) public statement on the Austistici/Inventati Collective. You can find the original article on their website in Italian.

Autistic/Invented: Banca Etica strongly condemns the use of counterterrorism tools to target political opponents. Evaluations are underway to prevent the closure of the bank account following A/I's inclusion on the US list of terrorist organizations. 

 Tuesday, September 1, 2026

On Friday, August 28, 2026, news was released of the U.S. administration's decision to include the Italian collective Autistici/Inventati in the OFAC lists , as part of targeted actions to " counter the growing threat posed by violent far-left terrorist groups ." Autistici/Inventati is a Tuscan collective that develops independent IT services and provides email addresses, websites, blogs, and newsletters to other activists and collectives. The Autistici/Inventati association has been a Banca Etica account holder since 2018: the account has always been in good working order without raising any concerns regarding money laundering, so much so that it remains within the medium risk profile. Following the US administration's decision to include A/I among the terrorist organizations, Banca Etica contacted Autistici/Inventati to inform them that, in effect, the Bank is forced to raise its risk profile and temporarily suspend the operations of the current account pending further investigation and it is unfortunately likely that it will soon be forced to close it.

Banca Etica is currently contacting the banking trade organizations (ABI; Assopopolari) and the Ministry of Economy and Finance to determine whether there are viable solutions that would allow Banca Etica to maintain the operations of Autistici/Inventati's current account without jeopardizing the operations of Banca Etica's other 130,000 customers and members. Banca Etica is also seeking further technical opinions to assess the scope of action allowed by the US measure.

In the absence of any pronouncement or guidance from Italian and European institutions on how a bank can protect itself in such cases, an Italian bank maintaining relationships with an OFAC-listed entity could be subject to "secondary sanctions" that would involve the cessation of all services provided by US intermediaries. This would mean that all Banca Etica customers would be unable to use credit and debit cards (which currently rely on a substantial monopoly by US operators) and would be unable to make payments in non-euro areas, which almost always require US financial intermediaries. Such an operational blockade would cause intolerable harm to the bank's customers and jeopardize the very survival of the bank. 

Ethical Bank:

  • strongly condemns the use of OFAC listings for political purposes and the imposition of related sanctions outside of strict compliance with the original mandate of these measures, which were created to prosecute criminal and terrorist activities

  • calls once again and more forcefully for European and national political institutions to combat the abuse of these instruments, so that European citizens and organisations are not the target of improper use of these sanctions ;

  • Stresses the need to mitigate the impact of the current dominance of global digital financial infrastructures by large US operators, since the extreme interdependence of banking systems makes this type of unilateral sanctioning initiative de facto binding on European operators as well, even when it presents unlawful aspects that harm European citizens or entities.

These are crucial issues for democracy and respect for human rights, on which Banca Etica, together with the European Federation of Ethical and Alternative Banks , has been seeking answers from Italian and European institutions for months, ever since the US added the UN Special Rapporteur for the Palestinian Territories and the judges of the International Criminal Court to the OFAC lists. Banca Etica will continue to do its part to stimulate international and institutional mobilization to end this unacceptable practice of targeting those whose political views differ from those of the current US administration, equating them with terrorists and effectively excluding them from the financial system.

items.title: History of the Harbor's Homeless
items.excerpt: Welcome to Molotov Now! This is Sprout, and this is Charyan, we are the hosts of Molotov Now!, and thank you for joining us on this episode of the podcast. In this two part episode we discuss and analyze many articles written by the local Daily World on the road the City of Aberdeen took to evict and traumatize a community on the banks of the Chehalis River known as the River Camp.  In part two, we will also look at the archives of the Harbor Rat Report, a deep dive on the local happenings and radical activism on the Harbor over the last two years. We have music from The Window Smashing J

items.title: Interview with Dr. Aaron Goings
items.excerpt: Welcome to Molotov Now! This is Sprout, and this is Charyan, we are the hosts of Molotov Now!, and thank you for joining us on this episode of the podcast. In this episode we talk to Dr. Aaron Goings, Associate professor of History at Saint Martin's University about his recent presentation at the 3rd annual May Day on the Harbor, held here in Hoquiam, WA. We discuss his work on researching the history of the town he once lived in, and try to tease out some lessons to be learned from that history that we can use in our current labor struggles. We have music from The Window Smashing Job Creators

Welcome to Molotov Now! This is Sprout, and this is Charyan, we are the hosts of Molotov Now!, and thank you for joining us on this episode of the podcast.


This time we are joined for two interviews, one with two organizers of a recent successful community defense action covering the first Pride event in Oregon City, and another with organizers of the upcoming Dual Power Gathering Midwest being held in Chicago August 17th to the 20th. This episode is all about the threats facing marginalized communities and the alternative power structures being built to liberate them.


We have music from sole and Rubella Ballet, a new audio newsletter, as well as a monthly radical news roundup.


Hope you enjoy.


Solidarity

This is Sprout and this is Charyan, and we are the hosts of Molotov Now!, on The Channel Zero Podcast Network, thank you for joining us on this episode of the podcast. If you like what we do here and want to support it, you can do that by going to linktr.ee/al1312 and clicking donate, or scrolling to the bottom for Patreon. Today on the podcast we are joined by a member of PDX Jail Support to discuss their efforts creating a culture of mutual aid based around the idea of widespread community jail support. They have spent the last four years building a network of volunteers to stand outside local jails and connect with people coming out of jail. This is done with all arrestees, not simply when there is a need for increased jail support following a protest event. We will also be debuting the audiozine we collaborated on with them detailing how to build a jail support network where you live. We hope you find this episode as inspiring as we did. It really lit a fire in us to get something similar going here where we live. The potential for radicalization is immense in these highly vulnerable and personal connections.

This is Sprout, and this is Charyan, and we are the hosts of Molotov Now!, on The Channel Zero Podcast Network, thank you for joining us on this episode of the podcast. If you like what we do here and want to support it, you can do that by going to linktr.ee/al1312 and clicking donate.


We are returning to you after a hiatus over the summer that saw us putting our writing hats down for some extended real world organizing.We have a lot to cover in this episode, having been gone for so long. We are choosing to forgo a guest spot this time in favor of recapping in detail the last few months of life here in Aberdeen, WA. What this has meant for organizing, the war on the unhoused, and local City politics.


That's right, from genocidal City policies towards the unhoused in town, to revelations about child molestation from the same City councilor responsible for doxxing a local mutual aid organizer recently.


Stay tuned for that discussion plus a radical news run down, music, and an audio version of our newsletter The Communique, catching you up on all the relevant happenings in Grays Harbor County Washington.
