items.title: Grays Harbor SOS
items.body:
Dispatches From the Rural Edge

 
"The county estimated between 500 and 3,000 unhoused people. The shelter had 25 beds."
 
We told our friends we would check back on them in the morning and left them out in the snow. Two were dead by morning. We lost a dozen friends that winter.
 
 Those numbers have been rattling around in our heads for years. Not because they are dramatic. Because they were true. The gap is where rural organizing happens. It is also why the number of people we lost was not even higher.
 
 Over the past several years Sabot Media has reported on housing, labor, mutual aid, homelessness, absentee landlords, shelter closures, development schemes, and local government failures. We have spoken with organizers from Texas to Gaza, from academics studying political polarization to Food Not Bombs chapters feeding people every week, and with people struggling to survive in places that rarely receive national attention.
 
 The details differed. The lesson rarely did.
 
 Again and again we encountered people solving enormous problems with remarkably few resources. During a Food Not Bombs roundtable discussion, organizers from Miami, Houston, West Palm Beach, Aberdeen, and elsewhere described dramatically different local conditions but remarkably similar challenges. The recurring problems were rarely ideological. They were practical. Reliable volunteers. Transportation. Burnout. Storage space. Keeping projects alive long enough to matter.
 
 When there are only six people willing to do the work, purity becomes a luxury. Relationships become infrastructure. Reliability becomes political. The question stops being whether everyone shares identical politics and becomes whether they will show up next week.

Throughout this report we use the words rural and urban in a very specific way.

When we say rural, we do not mean conservative. We do not mean Republican. We do not mean agricultural. We do not even necessarily mean small towns. Likewise, when we say urban, we do not mean liberal, Democratic, progressive, or radical. Research increasingly suggests those political labels are more strongly associated with geography and proximity to metropolitan centers than with fundamental differences in values.

Instead, we are describing organizational conditions.

Rural

Peripheral communities with lower population density, fewer institutions, fewer organizers, fewer resources, and greater distance between people. They often experience high needs but receive comparatively little attention or investment.

Urban

Major metropolitan areas with high population density, overlapping organizations, greater institutional capacity, more media attention, more funding, and a much larger concentration of organizers and movement infrastructure.

This distinction is not about culture.

It is not about political identity.

It is not about whether a community is radical.

It is about capacity.

A rural community may be politically conservative or politically radical. An urban neighborhood may be wealthy or desperately poor. Both can experience injustice. What differs is the density of people, institutions, and resources available to respond. That difference shapes how organizing works. Grays Harbor is not unique. That is precisely the problem.
 
 When Portland developer Terry Emmert began acquiring properties throughout Grays Harbor County, local residents learned a lesson familiar to rural communities throughout the country: some of the most important decisions affecting your town can be made by people who do not live there.
 
 Years ago we wrote:
 
 "So long as Terry Emmert maintains the illusion that he is investing into our city and 'fixing' these properties up, he is allowed to use them as tax shelters."


 Whether one agrees with every detail of that assessment is beside the point. The larger question remains: why does a developer living nearly two hundred miles away possess so much influence over housing conditions in a county he does not call home?
 
 Every rural community has its own version of this story. A developer. A corporation. An investment fund. A mining company. A timber company. An absentee landlord. The names change. The industries change. The dynamic remains.
 
 People often describe places like Grays Harbor as forgotten. That is not quite right. Forgotten implies nobody is paying attention. The reality is stranger. Rural communities are often intensely connected to the broader economy. Resources flow out. Wealth flows out. Young people leave. Decisions are made elsewhere. The profits go somewhere. The debts stay. The consequences stay.
 
 Housing is only one example.
 
 For years, local debates around homelessness in Grays Harbor have followed a familiar pattern. People living outside are moved from one location to another. Encampments are cleared. Vehicles are tagged and towed. Temporary solutions are proposed. Long-term solutions are promised. The conversation is forgotten. The crisis remains.
 
 At various points local governments have spent more resources debating where unhoused people should not exist rather than where they should. During winter storms, organizers and mutual aid groups repeatedly found themselves attempting to fill gaps that entire well-resourced institutions seemed unable or unwilling to address. The numbers changed from year to year. The underlying problem did not.
 
 As we wrote during one winter storm:
 
 "Needless to say the county's 25 bed shelter is insufficient to shelter even the lowest estimate."
 
 The lesson was difficult to ignore. The shortage was never just housing. It was capacity. Capacity to respond. Capacity to care. Capacity to imagine solutions beyond displacement.
 
 And so we ask a simple question: where did everything go?
 
 The jobs went somewhere. The investment went somewhere. The political attention went somewhere. The people went somewhere. The wealth certainly went somewhere. What remained were the consequences.
 
 The dominant story about rural America is usually cultural. En masse rural people vote differently. They watch different television. They drive different vehicles. They worship in different churches. They use different political labels. Entire industries now exist to explain these differences. Yet after years of reporting and organizing, we have become increasingly convinced that these explanations miss something important.
 
 Good people and assholes are distributed remarkably evenly across the landscape.
 
 We have worked alongside evangelical church volunteers, union members, anarchists, recovering addicts, old-fashioned veterans, curious teenagers, cop-loving queer liberals, conservative loggers, fishermen, teachers, and people who could not explain the difference between a socialist and a socialite if their lives depended on it. Some became trusted comrades. Some became obstacles. All turned out to be far more complicated than their labels suggested.
 
 A worker in Seattle may identify as progressive while a worker in Aberdeen identifies as conservative. One may distrust corporations while the other distrusts government. One may fly a pride flag while the other covers their truck in incoherent bumper stickers. Yet both may be struggling with housing costs, stagnant wages, inaccessible healthcare, childcare expenses, and the growing sense that decisions affecting their lives are being made somewhere else.
 
 The labels differ.
 
 The conditions often do not.
 
 Research increasingly supports this observation. Studies from Washington University in St. Louis suggest that proximity to major metropolitan centers and population density are among the strongest predictors of partisan identity. Other researchers have found that political attitudes frequently exist along a continuum rather than a simple rural-urban divide. Geography appears to shape political labels far more than many organizers assume.
 
 But labels are not values.
 
 That distinction matters because many radicals, including anarchists, often organize backwards. We begin with identity. We ask whether someone is an anarchist, socialist, conservative, liberal, progressive, or leftist before we understand what they actually believe.
 
 Saul Alinsky, a mid-20th century community organizer known for developing practical strategies for building grassroots power among working-class communities, understood something many organizers still struggle with. People rarely organize around theories. They organize around problems.
 
 We have known these people.
 
 A parent worried about rent who rejects every radical label but shows up to tenant meetings anyway. A logger who bristles at the word anarchist while talking for hours about absentee ownership and distant bureaucracies. A church volunteer who spends every weekend feeding hungry neighbors and insists they have no politics at all.
 
 Then someone introduces a label. Suddenly the conversation changes. Not because the values changed. Because the label entered the room. This presents anarchists with a challenge. If our goal is genuinely to build popular power, are we more committed to our values or our branding?
 
 Many of the people who could become our closest allies will never encounter anarchism through a book or a social media post. They will encounter it through a food distribution, a tenant campaign, a labor struggle, a disaster response, a community garden, or a mutual aid network. They will encounter it as a practice long before they encounter it as a label. The farther one moves from major metropolitan centers, the more obvious this becomes, as more and more of the people who show up are often not political radicals.
  

Part of the reason is scarcity.
 
 Cities operate under conditions of organizational abundance. There are more organizations, more activists, more events, more coalitions, more media outlets, more meeting spaces, and more opportunities to participate. This abundance creates opportunities, but it also creates fragmentation. When dozens of organizations occupy the same ecosystem, ideological distinction becomes a useful way to separate one group from another.
 
 Rural communities face a different reality.
 
 The challenge is not distinguishing between twenty organizations. The challenge is finding six people willing to consistently show up. Anyone who has spent time organizing in a rural community understands this intuitively. During our conversations with Food Not Bombs organizers, the recurring problem was rarely ideological. It was practical. Who has a vehicle? Who has a kitchen? Who can make it every week? Who can be counted on six months from now?
 
 In communities operating under conditions of scarcity, reliability often matters more than political precision because reliability is far harder to find.
 
 That changes everything.
 
 Relationships matter more. Reliability matters more. Capacity matters more. Organizers quickly learn that ideological sorting is a luxury. Coalition building becomes a necessity.
 
 This scarcity is reinforced by decades of brain drain. Young people leave for jobs, education, healthcare, culture, and opportunity concentrated elsewhere. Organizers leave because that is where movements appear to be happening. Resources follow them. Attention follows them. Networks follow them. Communities lose organizers because they lack organizing infrastructure and lack organizing infrastructure because they lose organizers.
 
 Grays Harbor offers a useful example of what scarcity looks like in practice. A handful of organizers often find themselves working across multiple projects simultaneously because there simply are not enough people available. The same person helping coordinate mutual aid may also be reporting local stories, attending city council meetings, supporting tenants, organizing events, distributing supplies, and maintaining relationships between groups that would otherwise have little contact with one another.
 
 This is not unique to the Harbor. Organizers we spoke with from Texas to Gaza described remarkably similar conditions. Yet the experience is especially visible in rural communities because there are fewer institutions available to absorb the pressure. When something breaks, there is often no larger organization waiting to step in.
 
 The work falls onto whoever remains. The results are visible in Grays Harbor. It is visible throughout the Rust Belt, Floridian swampland, flyover country, and in former mining towns, timber communities, agricultural regions, reservation lands, and struggling small towns throughout the country.
 
 The details differ.

The pattern remains.

A comrade recently relocated and had this to say about their experience:

“As a small-town Organizer moving to Seattle, the culture of resistance cultivated in the big city was its own form of culture shock, it is vastly larger and different from what I had experienced at home, in Aberdeen, WA.

I've seen things here that build the culture of resistance in the city more than I could ever dream possible in my hometown, community gardens and pantries, public venues and event spaces, large scale actions and protests, anarchist bookstores and bookfairs, workers and tenants’ unions, community meals and workshops, and so much more. But all these amazing projects and organizations are divided, be it by Ideology, Class, Scale, legality etc...

 Even the Anarchists seem further divided into various social cliques that feel much more isolated from each other than they should be. There is a weekly community meal I attend at a park in the city, at the time that it starts there are usually roughly 3-4 other organizations in the park at the same time also doing various forms of food distribution. They do not coordinate.

From churches bringing in various forms of donations and proselytism, to progressive liberal nonprofits bringing in clothes and PBS cameras, to anarchists throwing whatever food they are able to acquire that week legally or not on to a grill for the community. Even more so you have people making impromptu raves, LARPing troops, antifa kickball, and much more.

Yet, be it because of past conflicts or an aversion of working with organizations outside of those that comfortably fit within our own structures it seems there is absolutely zero communication between these organizations despite the exponential gains that could be gathered by working with each other, this is just simply not a luxury that we have in small towns.

Decentralization is a valid form of building dual power and a culture of resistance, but decentralization can only go so far without networking and communication. Networks like the ones in my hometown are in desperate need of communication and support from larger cities to give a booster shot from one culture of resistance to another, I fear how we can make this possible when city radicals are unable to network and communicate with themselves.”

~Seattle Based Anarchist


 NOTES ON ORG VS INDIVIDUAL

In Aberdeen, organizers spent years fighting over shelter beds, encampments, and basic survival while developers and politicians promised future solutions. During our Food Not Bombs roundtable, participants from dramatically different places kept returning to the same problems: too few volunteers, too little money, too little time, and too much work. Whether the conversation was happening in Texas, Gaza, Florida, Washington, or elsewhere, the geography changed. The conversation rarely did.
 
 The history of labor in Grays Harbor tells a similar story. Long before the current housing crisis, workers here were building unions, fighting timber barons, organizing through the Industrial Workers of the World, and struggling against concentrated economic power. The Harbor has never lacked for people willing to fight. What it has often lacked is the infrastructure necessary to sustain those fights across generations.
 
 That distinction matters.
 
 The problem facing many rural communities is not political apathy. It is organizational scarcity. There are people willing to do the work. There are not always enough resources to support them.
 
 For years Sabot has documented the consequences of scarcity in Grays Harbor. The purpose of this article is not to convince readers that those consequences exist. They already do. The question is what we intend to do about them. Grays Harbor does not need sympathy. It needs solidarity. All your rural comrades do.
 
 Not because these communities are uniquely deserving, but because they are attempting to solve enormous problems with remarkably few resources. A thousand dollars given to a large urban organization may barely register. The same thousand dollars can transform what is possible for a small rural project. The same is true of media attention, legal support, technical skills, research, transportation, design work, and human labor. Scarcity makes every resource matter more because there is so little margin for error.
 
 If you believe rural communities matter, then allocate resources accordingly.
 
 Fund rural media.
 Support rural organizers.
 Build relationships outside metropolitan centers.
 Visit.
 Report.
 Collaborate.
 Share skills.
 Send money.
 And when it makes sense, move.

EXPAND MOVING 

For decades, wealth, institutions, media attention, political power, and organizing infrastructure have all concentrated into the same metropolitan centers. Too often our movements have followed the same path. The result is that enormous portions of the country are treated as recruiting grounds, campaign stops, or abstractions rather than places where lasting movement infrastructure should be built.
 
 That concentration is not inevitable.
 
 It is a choice.
 
 Grays Harbor is sending an SOS.
 
 So are communities throughout Appalachia, on the Navajo Nation, across the Delta, in former timber towns, mining communities, agricultural regions, and hundreds of places that rarely appear in movement strategy discussions except as abstractions.
 
 The signal is already being sent.
 
 The question is whether we continue concentrating our movements in the same places as wealth and power, or whether we begin building them in the places those forces have spent decades abandoning.

items.bodyHtml:
Dispatches From the Rural Edge

 
"The county estimated between 500 and 3,000 unhoused people. The shelter had 25 beds."
 
We told our friends we would check back on them in the morning and left them out in the snow. Two were dead by morning. We lost a dozen friends that winter.
 
 Those numbers have been rattling around in our heads for years. Not because they are dramatic. Because they were true. The gap is where rural organizing happens. It is also why the number of people we lost was not even higher.
 
 Over the past several years Sabot Media has reported on housing, labor, mutual aid, homelessness, absentee landlords, shelter closures, development schemes, and local government failures. We have spoken with organizers from Texas to Gaza, from academics studying political polarization to Food Not Bombs chapters feeding people every week, and with people struggling to survive in places that rarely receive national attention.
 
 The details differed. The lesson rarely did.
 
 Again and again we encountered people solving enormous problems with remarkably few resources. During a Food Not Bombs roundtable discussion, organizers from Miami, Houston, West Palm Beach, Aberdeen, and elsewhere described dramatically different local conditions but remarkably similar challenges. The recurring problems were rarely ideological. They were practical. Reliable volunteers. Transportation. Burnout. Storage space. Keeping projects alive long enough to matter.
 
 When there are only six people willing to do the work, purity becomes a luxury. Relationships become infrastructure. Reliability becomes political. The question stops being whether everyone shares identical politics and becomes whether they will show up next week.

Throughout this report we use the words rural and urban in a very specific way.

When we say rural, we do not mean conservative. We do not mean Republican. We do not mean agricultural. We do not even necessarily mean small towns. Likewise, when we say urban, we do not mean liberal, Democratic, progressive, or radical. Research increasingly suggests those political labels are more strongly associated with geography and proximity to metropolitan centers than with fundamental differences in values.

Instead, we are describing organizational conditions.

Rural

Peripheral communities with lower population density, fewer institutions, fewer organizers, fewer resources, and greater distance between people. They often experience high needs but receive comparatively little attention or investment.

Urban

Major metropolitan areas with high population density, overlapping organizations, greater institutional capacity, more media attention, more funding, and a much larger concentration of organizers and movement infrastructure.

This distinction is not about culture.

It is not about political identity.

It is not about whether a community is radical.

It is about capacity.

A rural community may be politically conservative or politically radical. An urban neighborhood may be wealthy or desperately poor. Both can experience injustice. What differs is the density of people, institutions, and resources available to respond. That difference shapes how organizing works. Grays Harbor is not unique. That is precisely the problem.
 
 When Portland developer Terry Emmert began acquiring properties throughout Grays Harbor County, local residents learned a lesson familiar to rural communities throughout the country: some of the most important decisions affecting your town can be made by people who do not live there.
 
 Years ago we wrote:
 
 "So long as Terry Emmert maintains the illusion that he is investing into our city and 'fixing' these properties up, he is allowed to use them as tax shelters."


 Whether one agrees with every detail of that assessment is beside the point. The larger question remains: why does a developer living nearly two hundred miles away possess so much influence over housing conditions in a county he does not call home?
 
 Every rural community has its own version of this story. A developer. A corporation. An investment fund. A mining company. A timber company. An absentee landlord. The names change. The industries change. The dynamic remains.
 
 People often describe places like Grays Harbor as forgotten. That is not quite right. Forgotten implies nobody is paying attention. The reality is stranger. Rural communities are often intensely connected to the broader economy. Resources flow out. Wealth flows out. Young people leave. Decisions are made elsewhere. The profits go somewhere. The debts stay. The consequences stay.
 
 Housing is only one example.
 
 For years, local debates around homelessness in Grays Harbor have followed a familiar pattern. People living outside are moved from one location to another. Encampments are cleared. Vehicles are tagged and towed. Temporary solutions are proposed. Long-term solutions are promised. The conversation is forgotten. The crisis remains.
 
 At various points local governments have spent more resources debating where unhoused people should not exist rather than where they should. During winter storms, organizers and mutual aid groups repeatedly found themselves attempting to fill gaps that entire well-resourced institutions seemed unable or unwilling to address. The numbers changed from year to year. The underlying problem did not.
 
 As we wrote during one winter storm:
 
 "Needless to say the county's 25 bed shelter is insufficient to shelter even the lowest estimate."
 
 The lesson was difficult to ignore. The shortage was never just housing. It was capacity. Capacity to respond. Capacity to care. Capacity to imagine solutions beyond displacement.
 
 And so we ask a simple question: where did everything go?
 
 The jobs went somewhere. The investment went somewhere. The political attention went somewhere. The people went somewhere. The wealth certainly went somewhere. What remained were the consequences.
 
 The dominant story about rural America is usually cultural. En masse rural people vote differently. They watch different television. They drive different vehicles. They worship in different churches. They use different political labels. Entire industries now exist to explain these differences. Yet after years of reporting and organizing, we have become increasingly convinced that these explanations miss something important.
 
 Good people and assholes are distributed remarkably evenly across the landscape.
 
 We have worked alongside evangelical church volunteers, union members, anarchists, recovering addicts, old-fashioned veterans, curious teenagers, cop-loving queer liberals, conservative loggers, fishermen, teachers, and people who could not explain the difference between a socialist and a socialite if their lives depended on it. Some became trusted comrades. Some became obstacles. All turned out to be far more complicated than their labels suggested.
 
 A worker in Seattle may identify as progressive while a worker in Aberdeen identifies as conservative. One may distrust corporations while the other distrusts government. One may fly a pride flag while the other covers their truck in incoherent bumper stickers. Yet both may be struggling with housing costs, stagnant wages, inaccessible healthcare, childcare expenses, and the growing sense that decisions affecting their lives are being made somewhere else.
 
 The labels differ.
 
 The conditions often do not.
 
 Research increasingly supports this observation. Studies from Washington University in St. Louis suggest that proximity to major metropolitan centers and population density are among the strongest predictors of partisan identity. Other researchers have found that political attitudes frequently exist along a continuum rather than a simple rural-urban divide. Geography appears to shape political labels far more than many organizers assume.
 
 But labels are not values.
 
 That distinction matters because many radicals, including anarchists, often organize backwards. We begin with identity. We ask whether someone is an anarchist, socialist, conservative, liberal, progressive, or leftist before we understand what they actually believe.
 
 Saul Alinsky, a mid-20th century community organizer known for developing practical strategies for building grassroots power among working-class communities, understood something many organizers still struggle with. People rarely organize around theories. They organize around problems.
 
 We have known these people.
 
 A parent worried about rent who rejects every radical label but shows up to tenant meetings anyway. A logger who bristles at the word anarchist while talking for hours about absentee ownership and distant bureaucracies. A church volunteer who spends every weekend feeding hungry neighbors and insists they have no politics at all.
 
 Then someone introduces a label. Suddenly the conversation changes. Not because the values changed. Because the label entered the room. This presents anarchists with a challenge. If our goal is genuinely to build popular power, are we more committed to our values or our branding?
 
 Many of the people who could become our closest allies will never encounter anarchism through a book or a social media post. They will encounter it through a food distribution, a tenant campaign, a labor struggle, a disaster response, a community garden, or a mutual aid network. They will encounter it as a practice long before they encounter it as a label. The farther one moves from major metropolitan centers, the more obvious this becomes, as more and more of the people who show up are often not political radicals.
  

Part of the reason is scarcity.
 
 Cities operate under conditions of organizational abundance. There are more organizations, more activists, more events, more coalitions, more media outlets, more meeting spaces, and more opportunities to participate. This abundance creates opportunities, but it also creates fragmentation. When dozens of organizations occupy the same ecosystem, ideological distinction becomes a useful way to separate one group from another.
 
 Rural communities face a different reality.
 
 The challenge is not distinguishing between twenty organizations. The challenge is finding six people willing to consistently show up. Anyone who has spent time organizing in a rural community understands this intuitively. During our conversations with Food Not Bombs organizers, the recurring problem was rarely ideological. It was practical. Who has a vehicle? Who has a kitchen? Who can make it every week? Who can be counted on six months from now?
 
 In communities operating under conditions of scarcity, reliability often matters more than political precision because reliability is far harder to find.
 
 That changes everything.
 
 Relationships matter more. Reliability matters more. Capacity matters more. Organizers quickly learn that ideological sorting is a luxury. Coalition building becomes a necessity.
 
 This scarcity is reinforced by decades of brain drain. Young people leave for jobs, education, healthcare, culture, and opportunity concentrated elsewhere. Organizers leave because that is where movements appear to be happening. Resources follow them. Attention follows them. Networks follow them. Communities lose organizers because they lack organizing infrastructure and lack organizing infrastructure because they lose organizers.
 
 Grays Harbor offers a useful example of what scarcity looks like in practice. A handful of organizers often find themselves working across multiple projects simultaneously because there simply are not enough people available. The same person helping coordinate mutual aid may also be reporting local stories, attending city council meetings, supporting tenants, organizing events, distributing supplies, and maintaining relationships between groups that would otherwise have little contact with one another.
 
 This is not unique to the Harbor. Organizers we spoke with from Texas to Gaza described remarkably similar conditions. Yet the experience is especially visible in rural communities because there are fewer institutions available to absorb the pressure. When something breaks, there is often no larger organization waiting to step in.
 
 The work falls onto whoever remains. The results are visible in Grays Harbor. It is visible throughout the Rust Belt, Floridian swampland, flyover country, and in former mining towns, timber communities, agricultural regions, reservation lands, and struggling small towns throughout the country.
 
 The details differ.

The pattern remains.

A comrade recently relocated and had this to say about their experience:

“As a small-town Organizer moving to Seattle, the culture of resistance cultivated in the big city was its own form of culture shock, it is vastly larger and different from what I had experienced at home, in Aberdeen, WA.

I've seen things here that build the culture of resistance in the city more than I could ever dream possible in my hometown, community gardens and pantries, public venues and event spaces, large scale actions and protests, anarchist bookstores and bookfairs, workers and tenants’ unions, community meals and workshops, and so much more. But all these amazing projects and organizations are divided, be it by Ideology, Class, Scale, legality etc...

 Even the Anarchists seem further divided into various social cliques that feel much more isolated from each other than they should be. There is a weekly community meal I attend at a park in the city, at the time that it starts there are usually roughly 3-4 other organizations in the park at the same time also doing various forms of food distribution. They do not coordinate.

From churches bringing in various forms of donations and proselytism, to progressive liberal nonprofits bringing in clothes and PBS cameras, to anarchists throwing whatever food they are able to acquire that week legally or not on to a grill for the community. Even more so you have people making impromptu raves, LARPing troops, antifa kickball, and much more.

Yet, be it because of past conflicts or an aversion of working with organizations outside of those that comfortably fit within our own structures it seems there is absolutely zero communication between these organizations despite the exponential gains that could be gathered by working with each other, this is just simply not a luxury that we have in small towns.

Decentralization is a valid form of building dual power and a culture of resistance, but decentralization can only go so far without networking and communication. Networks like the ones in my hometown are in desperate need of communication and support from larger cities to give a booster shot from one culture of resistance to another, I fear how we can make this possible when city radicals are unable to network and communicate with themselves.”

~Seattle Based Anarchist


 NOTES ON ORG VS INDIVIDUAL

In Aberdeen, organizers spent years fighting over shelter beds, encampments, and basic survival while developers and politicians promised future solutions. During our Food Not Bombs roundtable, participants from dramatically different places kept returning to the same problems: too few volunteers, too little money, too little time, and too much work. Whether the conversation was happening in Texas, Gaza, Florida, Washington, or elsewhere, the geography changed. The conversation rarely did.
 
 The history of labor in Grays Harbor tells a similar story. Long before the current housing crisis, workers here were building unions, fighting timber barons, organizing through the Industrial Workers of the World, and struggling against concentrated economic power. The Harbor has never lacked for people willing to fight. What it has often lacked is the infrastructure necessary to sustain those fights across generations.
 
 That distinction matters.
 
 The problem facing many rural communities is not political apathy. It is organizational scarcity. There are people willing to do the work. There are not always enough resources to support them.
 
 For years Sabot has documented the consequences of scarcity in Grays Harbor. The purpose of this article is not to convince readers that those consequences exist. They already do. The question is what we intend to do about them. Grays Harbor does not need sympathy. It needs solidarity. All your rural comrades do.
 
 Not because these communities are uniquely deserving, but because they are attempting to solve enormous problems with remarkably few resources. A thousand dollars given to a large urban organization may barely register. The same thousand dollars can transform what is possible for a small rural project. The same is true of media attention, legal support, technical skills, research, transportation, design work, and human labor. Scarcity makes every resource matter more because there is so little margin for error.
 
 If you believe rural communities matter, then allocate resources accordingly.
 
 Fund rural media.
 Support rural organizers.
 Build relationships outside metropolitan centers.
 Visit.
 Report.
 Collaborate.
 Share skills.
 Send money.
 And when it makes sense, move.

EXPAND MOVING 

For decades, wealth, institutions, media attention, political power, and organizing infrastructure have all concentrated into the same metropolitan centers. Too often our movements have followed the same path. The result is that enormous portions of the country are treated as recruiting grounds, campaign stops, or abstractions rather than places where lasting movement infrastructure should be built.

 It is a choice.
 
 Grays Harbor is sending an SOS.
 
 So are communities throughout Appalachia, on the Navajo Nation, across the Delta, in former timber towns, mining communities, agricultural regions, and hundreds of places that rarely appear in movement strategy discussions except as abstractions.
 
 The signal is already being sent.
 
 The question is whether we continue concentrating our movements in the same places as wealth and power, or whether we begin building them in the places those forces have spent decades abandoning.

A/I says the decision leaves it unable to meet administrative obligations, pay service providers, or continue providing services.

timeline.body: A/I announces that the collective is shutting down and will discontinue all services shortly. It says continuing to operate under the current political and financial pressure would endanger users and the communities around it.

faq.question: What is Autistici/Inventati?
faq.answer: A/I is an Italian volunteer technology collective that has provided noncommercial communications infrastructure, including services associated with Noblogs. The reporting linked on this page contains the fuller history and sourcing.

faq.question: Why does this matter beyond one collective?
faq.answer: The campaign focuses on the distinction between communications infrastructure and the conduct of users. Privacy-preserving hosts, independent publishers, journalists, researchers, organizers, and civil-society projects all depend on that distinction remaining meaningful.

faq.question: Is Sabot Media affiliated with A/I?
faq.answer: No. Sabot Media and We Will Free Us are independent publishers and campaign organizers. They do not represent or speak for A/I.

faq.question: Is the monitor operated by Sabot?
faq.answer: No. Sabot reads the public A/I status page at kuma.accol.li and presents a compact summary here. The original monitor remains the authoritative view of its own data.

autistici-inventati.deck: A living campaign hub for reporting, public letters, graphics, press coverage, social circulation, infrastructure status, and ways to act before September 25.
autistici-inventati.summary: Sabot Media is independently documenting and opposing the treatment of resistant communications infrastructure as terrorism. This page gathers the campaign in one place and will remain as a public archive after the deadline.
autistici-inventati.disclaimer: Sabot Media is an independent publisher. We are not affiliated with Autistici/Inventati and do not represent or speak on behalf of A/I. Campaign material is political advocacy and reporting, not legal advice.

updates.title: U.S. designation announced
updates.body: The Treasury and State departments announce the designation of Autistici/Inventati, beginning the sanctions wind-down period.

updates.title: A/I responds publicly
updates.body: Autistici/Inventati rejects the allegations, defends antifascism and anticapitalism, and says the collective will continue providing digital self-defense infrastructure.

updates.title: The Server Called Paranoia published
updates.body: Sabot Media publishes the core investigation, historical context and source record for the campaign.

updates.title: Organizational open letter published

updates.title: Individual action letter released
updates.body: A printable letter template and recipient guide are released for direct advocacy in the United States, European Union, Italy and elsewhere.

updates.title: Campaign media kit released
updates.body: Twenty-two campaign graphics, full-resolution downloads, alt text and captions are collected for public circulation.

updates.title: A/I press briefing documents cascading impacts

updates.title: A/I reports partial restoration and financial-service pressure
updates.body: A/I reports that mail access has returned for almost all users and Noblogs is online read-only while technicians continue restoration. The collective also reports banking and PayPal consequences following the designation.

social.text: A/I may be ending. The story is nowhere near over. For twenty-five years, # AutisticiInventati showed what it could mean for movements to build and control their own communications infrastructure. Its loss should not send everyone searching for the next single service to replace it. It should send us looking in a hundred directions. In Boise, the Boise Autonomous Solidarity Hub is experimenting with one of them. @ BASH has put a small independent publication on NomadNet, a system running over Reticulum rather than relying solely on the conventional web. It has articles, archives, submissions and contact functions, reachable through a cryptographic network destination instead of an ordinary domain. 99a904b9ab830b7baa9d5115eb8854d7:/page/index.mu That is not the answer. That's what makes it interesting. Other projects are trying other things: cooperative infrastructure, self-managed servers, RSS, mirrors, print, radio, downloadable archives, federated publishing and networks that barely resemble the commercial web at all. We don't need to find another A/I. We need to understand how to build a thousand different pieces of what made A/I possible. Sabot is beginning a living guide to autonomous media and infrastructure, aimed especially at small and rural projects: how to publish, archive, distribute, host, mirror and keep going when a platform, host, domain, provider or collective disappears. Coming Soon: BECOME THE THOUSAND SERVERS A living guide to autonomous publishing, infrastructure and survival Follow the people experimenting. Follow small radical media. Preserve what matters. Then build something.

social.text: Nineteen days before the U.S. sanctions deadline, Autistici/Inventati is shutting down. For twenty-five years, A/I built infrastructure for people who understood that privacy, autonomy and resistance require more than good intentions. Now a government order has made keeping that infrastructure alive untenable. There is grief in this. There should also be fury. Because fascism does not arrive only as boots in the street. Sometimes it arrives as a designation, a compliance deadline, a terrified service provider, a bank account that suddenly stops working. Bureaucracy has always been one of authoritarianism’s favorite costumes. The paperwork looks terribly respectable while the walls close in. And this cannot remain a problem for “the nerds.” People organizing in every sphere need to understand what autonomous infrastructure means, why it matters, and what happens when we leave it to a tiny number of exhausted technical collectives to keep the lights on for everyone else. We need to become the thousand servers. Now. If one autonomous project can be isolated, there should be ten more behind it. A hundred. A thousand. This should be the moment radical hosting, federated services, community servers, privacy infrastructure and collectively controlled networks begin flourishing, not retreating. Build them in basements, social centers, infoshops, collectives, cooperatives and wherever else people can keep a machine humming and a cable plugged into the wall. The lesson cannot be that autonomous infrastructure was too dangerous to maintain. The lesson has to be that we did not have nearly enough of it. We ❤️ A/I. We are heartbroken to see it end this way. And we refuse to treat its shutdown as the end of the idea it spent twenty-five years proving was possible. Use the logo and banner provided by @ subvertising to keep their memory alive. Let's not forget this by next week! Goodbye, A/I. Not farewell. social.text: Press release from A/I A/I shuts down - Stay human Sep 6, 2026 The day we discovered we had been designated a global terrorist organization, we promised that we would try to resist as long as this was possible, that we would not back down as long as we could see options to stand our ground. For years, we have proudly maintained and defended a free, privacy-friendly, autonomous and politically committed infrastructure. “Stay human” is not an empty phrase to us. It means, above all, that we have a responsibility to protect our users, those who build the human networks we rely, and for the communities who flooded us with messages of support and solidarity. We cannot engage in a fight or expose ourselves to manipulations that threaten the lives of these people and their loved ones, leaving them at the mercy of autocrats, fascists and agencies that take extra-legal courses of action. The possibility that our work may cause legal and financial consequences to those who are close to us - or even only have something to do with us - leaves us no choice. A/I is shutting down. The Autistici/Inventati collective is shutting down and will soon discontinue all of the services we provide. There is no easy way to announce or explain this Every day we stayed online after August 26, 2026, has been a victory, but now we are forced to stop. None of us holds eroic gestures and martyrs in high esteem, therefore we will demand no sacrifices. Not from us, not from anyone else. In this political climate, continuing to offer our services endangers our users and anyone who is part of our communities. In a world where allegations are disconnected from reality, we can only expect repression to be increasingly disproportionate. Under these circumstances, we are no longer able to maintain our original mission - offering secure and non-commercial digital tools. These 25 years have been amazing. It’s been an “incredible ride”. Now turn off your PCs, get out of your homes, struggle, hug each other and keep on smiling. We are stopping, but the Resistance and ideas do not stop. Stay human. We will soon send instructions on how to back up the content of your blogs, mailboxes and websites, along with more technical recommendations. But keep in mind that, just as the autistici.org domain was made unreachable without previous notice, in the next few days we might suffer similar issues that we may not be able to predict. Autistici/Inventati Collective

social.text: Andy Ngo has publicly asked the U.S. State Department to treat Sabot Media’s reporting on the Autistici/Inventati sanctions as “support” for A/I and has described this publication as its “propaganda wing.” Sabot Media is an independent publication. We are not an agent, affiliate or organizational arm of Autistici/Inventati. We have reported on the U.S. government’s designation, interviewed affected parties, examined the people and institutions that advocated for the policy, and published the underlying records so readers can evaluate them for themselves. That is journalism. It is also worth noting that OFAC’s own guidance states that U.S. sanctions do not prohibit constitutionally protected political speech and recognizes protections for the exchange of information and informational materials. If Ngo or Kyle Shideler has evidence that Sabot Media has provided financial, technical or other prohibited services to A/I, they should publish it. signatories.statement: BMorePunk stands in solidarity with A/I. Publishing the speech of others is not terrorism. Independent hosting collectives must all take a united stand against this outrageous injustice. An injury to one is an injury to all.

signatories.name: Restore The Fourth
signatories.statement: Privacy, encryption, pseudonymity and refusal to retain unnecessary identifying data are not evidence of terrorism. They are only evidence of human beings communicating, organizing and thriving without the State peering over their shoulder. Warrantless data-gathering partnerships between corporations and the State have the power to extinguish any real dissent. We all desperately need means of organizing and communication that are neither controlled by Big Tech, nor readily monitored by governments.

signatories.statement: Speak out. Support Autistici. Support independent, movement-aligned technology and defend our ability to communicate, organize, and build community power outside the claws of Big Tech.

signatories.name: Minnesota Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers
signatories.statement: MACDL supports free speech, dissent, and the right to communicate without being compelled to include the US government in our communications. The Fourth Amendment was created to keep the government out of our private affairs. This illegal action also implicates the right to remain silent.

signatories.name: Bonfire Networks
signatories.statement: A/I's mission has always been clear, and for more than twenty years it has inspired generations of hackers and activists in Italy and around the world: "Socializzare saperi senza fondare poteri." Sharing knowledge without establishing power. That is what the US is attacking, and that is what is at stake today. The premise of these sanctions, that whoever provides communications infrastructure answers for whatever anyone does with it, would criminalise and shut down most Big Tech platforms tomorrow if applied equally. Instead it is aimed at grassroots services who refuse to surveil their users. We condemn these sanctions, and we stand firmly with solidarity tech like A/I. Antifascism and anticapitalism are not terrorism.

signatories.name: Ukrudt.net
signatories.statement: As both users, supporters, and kin of Autistici/Inventati - sharing the cause of running autonomous infrastructure with a similar ethos (anti-capitalist, anti-militarist, feminist, fighting against repression on the internet for initiatives under political pressure) and built on FLOSS (Free/Libre Open Source Software) - we accuse the US government of censorship and digital repression, and stand in full solidarity with Autistici/Inventati. We will continue caring for our own infrastructure and working for the sprouting of autonomous, anti-capitalist, and anti-fascist server kinships, and we see the US designation ofAutistici/Inventati as a direct attack on our cause. We urge all actors to pressure the US government to lift it’s sanctions on Autistici/Inventati.

signatories.name: Geeks For Social Change
signatories.statement: Corporations are currently attempting to conspire with governments to entirely eliminate the independent web and have our lives be entirely mediated by billionaires. This censorship of A/I is a dangerous step towards making it impossible to voice political dissent online and must be stopped.

signatories.statement: Many of our allies & friends in South East Asia use Autistici/Inventati services to protect themselves from state suppression of their speech, often other platforms will comply with takedown requests from authoritarian regimes and the platform provided by Autistici/Inventati are a lifeline. The sanctions by the US are a threat to their ability to speak freely to the world. Moreover the sanctions are unjustified as Autistici/Inventati are merely a infrastructure provider, they have done nothing wrong that any other email provider, blog host or social media platform has not also done.

signatories.name: Datenpunks e.V.
signatories.statement: Indyhosters and tech collectives like Autistici/Inventati play an important role in democratic societies: By providing tracking-free online services, they show that privacy-preserving communication is possible even though Big Tech and some governments want us to believe otherwise. In doing so, volunteer-run collectives such as A/I protect marginalized communities from surveillance capitalism and authoritarian governments. Everyone who cares about human rights should support them.

signatories.name: Jeremy Beausoleil Smith
signatories.statement: This fascistic attack on our freedom of speech is unacceptable and must be undone. This is a targeted act of suppression against anyone standing up to Trump and his administration’s attempts to destroy our Democracy. The United States government is setting a dangerous precedent that will allow for further censorship and erosion of our Civil Rights. I oppose expansion of the surveillance state locally here in Portland, the United States, and globally. We deserve a future free from unfettered government and corporate surveillance.

timeline.title: Autistici/Inventati is formed
timeline.body: People and collectives working on technology, privacy, cyber-rights and political activism meet in Italy and begin building free, noncommercial communications tools. The first server is called Paranoia.

timeline.title: The first demand for user data
timeline.body: Investigators ask A/I for identifying information about mail users. Because the collective does not retain identity data or activity logs, it has nothing useful to hand over.

timeline.title: Trenitalia tries to silence a hosted site
timeline.body: The Italian railway company targets Zenmai, an A/I-hosted satire site criticizing military transport. The site is taken down during the dispute, but A/I ultimately wins the legal case.

timeline.title: Police compromise the Aruba server
timeline.body: Italian postal police shut down A/I’s server at commercial provider Aruba, copy material and obtain cryptographic keys without notifying the collective. The intervention potentially exposes communications far beyond the single mailbox under investigation.

timeline.title: A/I discovers the compromise
timeline.body: The collective learns of the secret 2004 intervention while reviewing legal records. It publicly documents the breach and warns users that no infrastructure provider can replace personal encryption practices.

timeline.title: The R* Plan goes public
timeline.body: A/I responds by distributing services across a resistant network of self-managed servers. Machines are designed to be replaceable, data is decentralized and a single seizure should no longer collapse the whole system.

timeline.title: Servers in three countries are seized
timeline.body: An investigation seeks logs A/I does not keep and triggers international requests involving servers in Norway, the Netherlands and Switzerland. Authorities recover encrypted files but no useful identifying information.

timeline.title: The United States designates A/I
timeline.body: The U.S. announces terrorism-related sanctions against the volunteer collective, treating shared communications infrastructure as a target because movements used the services it provided.

timeline.title: A/I documents cascading service pressure
timeline.body: A/I publishes an English-language briefing on the designation, the autistici.org DNS serverHold, reported pressure on banking and payment services, and the resulting risks to email, mailing lists, websites and blogs. The release distinguishes established facts from unresolved questions about who ordered each intervention.

timeline.title: A/I restores access while financial pressure grows
timeline.body: A/I reports that mail service is accessible again for almost all users and Noblogs is back online in read-only mode. The collective also reports that Banca Etica intends to close its banking relationship and that PayPal blocked its account.

timeline.title: The wind-down period ends
timeline.body: The temporary U.S. authorization expires at 12:01 a.m. Eastern. Banks, hosts, registrars, certificate providers and other intermediaries may face pressure to cut services or over-comply.

timeline.title: Public campaign launched
timeline.body: Reporting, public letters, journalist outreach, graphics, and direct advocacy begin circulating.

timeline.title: Banca Etica moves to close A/I’s account
timeline.body: On September 4, Banca Etica tells AI ODV it will unilaterally terminate the association’s bank account and that the donated funds remaining in it will not be available to the association. A/I says the decision leaves it unable to meet administrative obligations, pay service providers, or continue providing services.

timeline.title: A/I announces it is shutting down
timeline.body: A/I announces that the collective is shutting down and will discontinue all services shortly. It says continuing to operate under the current political and financial pressure would endanger users and the communities around it.

faq.question: What is Autistici/Inventati?
faq.answer: A/I is an Italian volunteer technology collective that has provided noncommercial communications infrastructure, including services associated with Noblogs. The reporting linked on this page contains the fuller history and sourcing.

faq.question: Why does this matter beyond one collective?
faq.answer: The campaign focuses on the distinction between communications infrastructure and the conduct of users. Privacy-preserving hosts, independent publishers, journalists, researchers, organizers, and civil-society projects all depend on that distinction remaining meaningful.

faq.question: Is Sabot Media affiliated with A/I?
faq.answer: No. Sabot Media is an independent publisher and does not represent or speak for A/I.

faq.question: Is the monitor operated by Sabot?
faq.answer: No. Sabot reads the public A/I status page at kuma.accol.li and presents a compact summary here. The original monitor remains the authoritative view of its own data.
